nameStory: The egg-yolk jelly gets its appetizing name from its distinctive appearance — a translucent white bell with a bright yellow-orange center that looks remarkably like a fried egg floating in the water. Some people call it the fried egg jellyfish for the same reason, though 'egg-yolk' better captures that golden central dome that really makes it stand out.
description: The egg-yolk jelly is one of the largest jellyfish you might encounter in New England waters, though sightings are quite rare here. This impressive creature has a translucent white bell that can grow up to 2 feet across, with a distinctive bright yellow or orange dome in the center that gives it its fried egg appearance. What makes it even more spectacular are its incredibly long tentacles — up to 20 feet long — that trail behind it in graceful, ribbon-like clusters.

idTips.label: Distinctive coloration
idTips.description: Look for the unmistakable fried egg pattern — a clear white, jelly-like bell with a bright yellow to orange dome in the center, just like a sunny-side-up egg

idTips.label: Massive size
idTips.description: This is a giant among jellies, with bells reaching up to 2 feet across — much larger than the common moon jellies you typically see

idTips.label: Tentacle clusters
idTips.description: Count about 16 distinct clusters of tentacles around the bell's edge, each cluster containing dozens of individual strands that can stretch incredibly long

idTips.label: Bell texture
idTips.description: The bell feels firm and gelatinous when washed ashore, with a smooth, almost rubbery texture that's thicker than typical moon jellies

idTips.label: Trailing tentacles
idTips.description: In the water, you'll see extremely long, flowing tentacles that can extend 20 feet or more, creating an impressive underwater curtain

habitat: Egg-yolk jellies are open ocean wanderers that occasionally drift into New England's coastal waters, particularly in deeper offshore areas. They prefer cooler waters and are most likely to be spotted from boats in the Gulf of Maine or washed up on beaches after storms. These jellies are rare visitors to our region, coming from the North Pacific or Arctic waters.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in New England waters during spring, though this would be when any specimens might begin drifting into our region with changing currents.
seasonality.summer: Most likely season to spot one in New England waters or washed up on beaches, particularly after storms that bring deep-water species closer to shore.
seasonality.fall: Occasional sightings possible as ocean currents shift, though specimens may show signs of deterioration from their long journey to our waters.
seasonality.winter: Extremely unlikely to encounter, as cold winter conditions and seasonal current patterns make appearances virtually impossible.

funFact: An egg-yolk jelly's tentacles can stretch longer than a school bus and contain millions of stinging cells, yet small fish often swim safely among them — the fish have developed immunity to the sting and use the jellyfish as a mobile fortress for protection from larger predators!
confusionNotes: You might confuse smaller egg-yolk jellies with moon jellies, but remember the 'breakfast test' — moon jellies are translucent white all over like egg whites, while egg-yolk jellies have that distinctive yellow-orange center that looks like you cracked an egg into the ocean.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'fried egg' jellyfish, there's actually another smaller species (Cotylorhiza tuberculata) in the Mediterranean that also goes by this name, which can cause confusion in field guides. The egg-yolk jelly is much larger and is primarily a cold-water species, making it quite rare in New England waters.
compareHints: The egg-yolk jelly is the only species in its genus and has no close relatives in New England waters. Compared to our common moon jellies, it's much larger, has the distinctive yellow center, and possesses far longer tentacles arranged in obvious clusters rather than the short, fine tentacles of moon jellies. It's truly in a class of its own when it comes to New England jellyfish.
